bibl.title: Development of Inhibitory Timescales in Auditory Cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how the timing of cortical inhibition matures over the weeks after hearing onset
span.quote: The time course of inhibition plays an important role in cortical sensitivity, tuning, and temporal response properties. We investigated the development of L2/3 inhibitory circuitry between fast-spiking (FS) interneurons and pyramidal cells (PCs) in auditory thalamocortical slices from mice between postnatal day 10 (P10) and P29.

span.label: which intrinsic and synaptic properties set the speed of inhibitory recruitment, and how each changes between P10 and P29
span.quote: In this study, we examine the development of L2/3 circuitry, which complements previous in vivo studies that focused on the thalamorecipient layers (L3–L5).

span.label: shows fast-spiking cells and their synapses both speed up over development, and that the temporal properties of inhibition mature later than those of excitation
span.quote: Finally, we show that during early development, the temporal properties that influence the recruitment of inhibition lag those of excitation.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: We found that the maturation of the intrinsic and synaptic properties of both FS cells and their connected PCs influence the timescales of inhibition.

span.label: postnatal development of inhibitory timing in auditory cortex layer 2/3
span.quote: We investigated the development of L2/3 inhibitory circuitry between fast-spiking (FS) interneurons and pyramidal cells (PCs) in auditory thalamocortical slices from mice between postnatal day 10 (P10) and P29.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Whole-cell current-clamp recordings were made from 116 FS cells that were synaptically connected to 134 PCs in L2/3 of AI.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Shortening of the postsynaptic membrane time constant during development speeds the decay of synaptic potentials
span.quote: These age-dependent decreases in τ d may, in part, be attributed to changes in the membrane time constant of the FS cells since the mean τ d and τ m at each age were linearly correlated ( R : 0.88, P < 0.01, Fig. 3 H ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Falling input resistance of the postsynaptic pyramidal cell offsets a rising inhibitory current, so the measured IPSP amplitude declines with age
span.quote: One likely explanation for our results is that correlated decreases in PC input resistance during development counter increases in IPSC amplitude.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Later IPSP peak times in young animals reduce excitation-inhibition overlap and thereby widen the synaptic integration window
span.quote: This would likely decrease overlap between EPSPs and IPSPs, broaden the integration window in young animals, and allow spike responses to nonoptimal or less precisely timed inputs.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Inhibitory decay constants longer than excitatory ones impose an upper frequency limit on responses to closely spaced inputs
span.quote: This suggests that inhibition sets an upper frequency bound for responses to inputs arriving at short intervals.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Developmental expression of leak and repolarizing potassium channels in PV+ FS cells drives the change in intrinsic excitability
span.quote: These changes coincide with the early development (P7–P25) of potassium channels in PV+ FS cells that contribute to leak (Kcnk3 and Kcnk1) and spike repolarization (Kv3 and Kcnn2) ( Du et al. 1996 ; Rudy and McBain 2001 ; Tansey et al. 2002 ; Okaty et al. 2009 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A switch from slow alpha-3 to faster alpha-1 GABA_A receptor subunits accelerates IPSP rise and decay
span.quote: However, the developmental transition from slow α 3 subunits in GABA A receptors to faster α 1 subunits may also contribute to changes in IPSP rise and decay times ( Gingrich et al. 1995 ; Xu et al. 2010 ).

span.label: faster firing in older cells follows from shorter membrane time constants, briefer afterhyperpolarisations and narrower spikes
span.quote: We found that the maturation of the intrinsic and synaptic properties of both FS cells and their connected PCs influence the timescales of inhibition. FS cell firing rates increased with age owing to decreased membrane time constants, shorter afterhyperpolarizations, and narrower action potentials.

span.label: the speed-up coincides with development of potassium channels handling leak and spike repolarisation
span.quote: These changes coincide with the early development (P7–P25) of potassium channels in PV+ FS cells that contribute to leak (Kcnk3 and Kcnk1) and spike repolarization (Kv3 and Kcnn2)

span.label: excitatory decay tracks the membrane time constant of the receiving cell, so a synaptic timescale is partly a membrane timescale
span.quote: At rest, the short duration EPSPs are consistent with predominantly AMPA receptor–mediated current and correlated with FS cell membrane time constants throughout development.

span.label: inhibitory rise, peak and decay times shorten with age, attributed in part to the falling membrane time constant of the receiving pyramidal cell
span.quote: The rise, peak, and decay times of the IPSPs decreased with age, which may, in part, be attributed to correlated decreases in membrane time constant of the postsynaptic PCs.

span.label: shorter inhibitory decays let older cells follow inputs at 20-40 Hz where younger ones summate and stop responding above 10 Hz
span.quote: We have shown that the decay constants of inhibitory synapses were significantly longer than excitation at all ages. This suggests that inhibition sets an upper frequency bound for responses to inputs arriving at short intervals. In young animals, IPSPs are approximately 60–200 ms long and can summate during repetitive ( Fig. 5 ) or asynchronous stimulation producing long-lasting hyperpolarizations that reduce responsiveness to frequencies >10 Hz. In older animals, decreased IPSP durations (25–50 ms) limit summation and increase neural responsiveness to higher input frequencies (20–40 Hz).

span.label: Voltage clamp was deliberately not used, limiting the measurements to current-clamp postsynaptic potentials.
span.quote: Voltage clamp recordings were not performed because the standard internal solutions required for adequate space clamp would prohibit the characterization of intrinsic neural properties as well as the ability to assess bidirectional connections.

span.label: Whether the paired-cell changes in inhibitory strength hold at the population level in vivo is unknown.
span.quote: It remains to be determined how changes in inhibitory strength between pairs of neurons are reflected at the population level in vivo.

span.label: The functional consequences for auditory processing were not tested and require in vivo work.
span.quote: Further in vivo studies are necessary to elucidate functional implications of the maturation of these circuit properties during auditory processing.

span.label: Identifying fast-spiking cells electrophysiologically is unreliable in the youngest animals.
span.quote: The identification of FS cells based on electrophysiological properties can be difficult particularly in young animals (P10–P14) since “FS” responses are less apparent.

span.label: voltage clamp was deliberately not used, because the solutions needed for it would have prevented measuring intrinsic properties and bidirectional connections
span.quote: Voltage clamp recordings were not performed because the standard internal solutions required for adequate space clamp would prohibit the characterization of intrinsic neural properties as well as the ability to assess bidirectional connections.

span.label: the age bins were divided arbitrarily
span.quote: The transitional period was divided arbitrarily into an early phase (P10–P14), which coincides with the critical period for tonotopic map organization in AI of rats ( de Villers-Sidani et al. 2007 ), and a later phase (P15–P18).

span.label: only postsynaptic potentials that fitted the double-exponential model well were analysed
span.quote: Only PSPs that were well fit by equation 1 (χ 2 < 1.75, n = 155 EPSPs, n = 167 IPSPs) were chosen

span.label: receptor composition changes are not excluded as an additional cause of the synaptic decay changes
span.quote: However, our results do not preclude the possibility that developmental changes in AMPA and/or NMDA receptor composition ( Lambolez et al. 1996 ; Kumar et al. 2002 ; Lu et al. 2007 ; Wang and Gao 2009 ) may also contribute to synaptic decays at higher resting potentials than we report

span.label: how paired-cell inhibitory strength maps onto the population level in the intact animal is left open
span.quote: It remains to be determined how changes in inhibitory strength between pairs of neurons are reflected at the population level in vivo.

span.label: a GFP line used not as the object of study but as a check on an electrophysiological classification
span.quote: Since the majority of FS interneurons are PV+ ( Kawaguchi and Kondo 2002 ) and G42 mice express the EGFP transgene in (PV+) cells, we compared the properties of GFP+ interneurons recorded from G42 mice with FS cells recorded in SW mice of the same age. We found that the intrinsic membrane properties and AP properties ( Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 1 ) of the FS cells in our dataset did not differ between G42 and SW mice at any age.

span.label: the expectation that a synaptic potential's time course follows the membrane time constant of the cell receiving it
span.quote: At rest, the short duration EPSPs are consistent with predominantly AMPA receptor–mediated current and correlated with FS cell membrane time constants throughout development.

span.label: EPSPs → FS cell membrane time constants
span.note: CORRELATED THROUGHOUT DEVELOPMENT, with no manipulation of either quantity. Recording it as `causes` in either direction asserts more than the sentence does.
span.quote: At rest, the short duration EPSPs are consistent with predominantly AMPA receptor–mediated current and correlated with FS cell membrane time constants throughout development.

span.label: FS is an ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL category whose defining features are absent in the youngest animals, which is exactly the age this paper is about
span.quote: The identification of FS cells based on electrophysiological properties can be difficult particularly in young animals (P10–P14) since “FS” responses are less apparent.

span.label: the transgenic label covers only a SUBSET - the PV cells that are also fast-spiking express EGFP - so GFP-positive is narrower than PV-positive
span.quote: In the G42 mice, the subset of PV+ cells that are FS express the EGFP transgene ( Chattopadhyaya et al. 2004 ) and fluoresce green

span.label: IPSP and IPSC are not interchangeable measures of inhibitory strength: they differ by the postsynaptic input resistance, which itself falls with age
span.quote: Alternatively, recent in vivo studies in AI have shown that inhibitory strength is stable throughout early development ( Dorrn et al. 2010 ; Sun et al. 2010 ). One likely explanation for our results is that correlated decreases in PC input resistance during development counter increases in IPSC amplitude.

span.label: reported PSP amplitudes are averaged over all trials INCLUDING failures, so they are a product of size and reliability rather than a size alone
span.quote: The reported PSP amplitudes are averaged over all trials and include failures.

span.label: a successful PSP is defined by a three-part criterion on onset, amplitude and peak time, with anything else counted as a failure of amplitude zero
span.quote: Presynaptic stimulation successfully evoked an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) or excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) if, 1) the onset of PSP was within 3 ms of the presynaptic action potential (AP) initiation; 2) the PSP amplitude (baseline to peak) was a minimum of 0.05 mV; or 3) the PSP peaked within 20 ms (IPSPs) or 7 ms (EPSPs) of onset. Otherwise, the trial was considered a failure with an “amplitude” of 0 mV.

span.label: extends → Oswald and Reyes 2008 (development of L2/3 pyramidal cells in AI)
span.quote: As previously shown for PCs ( Oswald and Reyes 2008 ), both the intrinsic and the synaptic properties of FS cells undergo a transition between P10 and P18 and plateau between P19 and P29.

span.label: builds-on → Oswald and Reyes 2008 (companion study on PC–PC circuitry)
span.quote: In closing, the results of this and our companion study ( Oswald and Reyes 2008 ) suggest that the developmental changes in the intrinsic and synaptic properties of PC–FS circuitry lead to faster timescales that can enhance precision and temporal responsiveness of neurons in L2/3.

span.label: contradicts → Doischer et al. 2008; Kobayashi et al. 2008 (age-related increase in IPSC amplitude in other cortical areas)
span.quote: These results were somewhat unexpected given that IPSC amplitudes in other cortical areas increase with age ( Doischer et al. 2008 ; Kobayashi et al. 2008 )

span.label: contradicts → Dorrn et al. 2010; Sun et al. 2010 (in vivo reports that inhibitory strength is stable in early development)
span.quote: Alternatively, recent in vivo studies in AI have shown that inhibitory strength is stable throughout early development ( Dorrn et al. 2010 ; Sun et al. 2010 ).

span.label: contradicts → reports from other cortical areas that inhibitory postsynaptic amplitudes increase with age
span.quote: There is also a modest but significant decrease in IPSP amplitude between P10 and P29. These results were somewhat unexpected given that IPSC amplitudes in other cortical areas increase with age ( Doischer et al. 2008 ; Kobayashi et al. 2008 ); α 1 GABA A receptor subunits have a higher peak current than α 3 subunits ( Gingrich et al. 1995 ) and GAD65 expression increases

span.label: reconciles → that disagreement, by proposing that falling input resistance converts a rising current into a falling voltage
span.quote: Alternatively, recent in vivo studies in AI have shown that inhibitory strength is stable throughout early development ( Dorrn et al. 2010 ; Sun et al. 2010 ). One likely explanation for our results is that correlated decreases in PC input resistance during development counter increases in IPSC amplitude.

span.label: extends → their own companion study on pyramidal cell development in the same layer
span.quote: As previously shown for PCs ( Oswald and Reyes 2008 ), both the intrinsic and the synaptic properties of FS cells undergo a transition between P10 and P18 and plateau between P19 and P29.

span.label: supports → the proposal that inhibitory tuning lags excitatory tuning, which the paper notes is itself disputed
span.quote: It has been suggested that the establishment of inhibitory tuning lags excitatory tuning ( Chang et al. 2005 ; Dorrn et al. 2010 ; but also see Sun et al. 2010

span.label: builds-on → in vivo work on thalamorecipient layers, by adding the supragranular circuit
span.quote: In this study, we examine the development of L2/3 circuitry, which complements previous in vivo studies that focused on the thalamorecipient layers (L3–L5).

span.label: IPSP —distinct-from→ IPSC
span.note: CRITERION: the two differ by input resistance, which falls with age - so the same inhibitory strength can appear to fall in voltage while rising in current. This is what resolves the disagreement with other cortical areas
span.quote: Alternatively, recent in vivo studies in AI have shown that inhibitory strength is stable throughout early development ( Dorrn et al. 2010 ; Sun et al. 2010 ). One likely explanation for our results is that correlated decreases in PC input resistance during development counter increases in IPSC amplitude.

span.label: input resistance —causes→ IPSP
span.note: the conversion factor between the measures is itself a developing variable, which is why a cross-paper comparison of inhibitory strength needs to know which was measured
span.quote: Alternatively, recent in vivo studies in AI have shown that inhibitory strength is stable throughout early development ( Dorrn et al. 2010 ; Sun et al. 2010 ). One likely explanation for our results is that correlated decreases in PC input resistance during development counter increases in IPSC amplitude.

span.label: RETRACTED (PLAIN CORRELATION) · membrane time constant —causes→ EPSP
span.note: RETRACTED: PLAIN CORRELATION. The span reports that short duration EPSPs are consistent with predominantly AMPA receptor-mediated current and CORRELATED WITH FS cell membrane time constants throughout development. It reports a covariation across development and no manipulation of either quantity. WHAT THE SPAN DOES SAY (Q-309): that correlation, housed below. — the excitatory decay tracks the membrane constant, so part of a synaptic timescale is a cellular one
span.quote: At rest, the short duration EPSPs are consistent with predominantly AMPA receptor–mediated current and correlated with FS cell membrane time constants throughout development.

span.label: membrane time constant —causes→ IPSP
span.note: same route on the inhibitory side, with a receptor subunit switch offered as an additional cause
span.quote: The rise, peak, and decay times of the IPSPs decreased with age, which may, in part, be attributed to correlated decreases in membrane time constant of the postsynaptic PCs.

span.label: GABA A —causes→ IPSP
span.note: the alpha-3 to alpha-1 switch; an alternative not separated from the membrane route here
span.quote: However, the developmental transition from slow α 3 subunits in GABA A receptors to faster α 1 subunits may also contribute to changes in IPSP rise and decay times

span.label: G42 —operationalised-as→ FS
span.note: CRITERION: GFP cells in the transgenic line matched electrophysiologically identified cells at every age, which is what licenses the classification where the electrophysiology is weakest
span.quote: Since the majority of FS interneurons are PV+ ( Kawaguchi and Kondo 2002 ) and G42 mice express the EGFP transgene in (PV+) cells, we compared the properties of GFP+ interneurons recorded from G42 mice with FS cells recorded in SW mice of the same age. We found that the intrinsic membrane properties and AP properties ( Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 1 ) of the FS cells in our dataset did not differ between G42 and SW mice at any age.

span.label: FS —contrasted-with→ PCs
span.note: the mature separation rests on firing rate, spike width and afterhyperpolarisation - all of which are absent before P15
span.quote: Typically, FS cells in older animals (P15–P18, P19–P29; Fig. 1 , middle, right) have suprathreshold electrophysiological features that distinguish them from PCs and other interneurons ( Connors and Gutnick 1990 ). These include high nonadapting firing rates (ISI Last :ISI First : 1.09 ± 0.14, see Methods), a high rheobase (∼0.3), and narrow action potentials (half width, HW: 0.2–0.5 ms), with strong, brief afterhyperpolarizations

span.label: IPSP —causes→ integration window
span.note: SIGN: later inhibitory peaks widen the window, so young cells accept less precisely timed inputs
span.quote: We have shown that IPSPs peak later in P10–P14 neurons than in P19–P29 neurons. This would likely decrease overlap between EPSPs and IPSPs, broaden the integration window in young animals, and allow spike responses to nonoptimal or less precisely timed inputs.

span.label: short-term depression —operationalised-as→ paired pulse ratio
span.quote: PC–FS synapses showed frequency-dependent short-term depression that decreased with age ( Fig. 3 B – D ). The paired pulse ratios (10-Hz stimulation; PPR = EPSP 2 /EPSP 1 ) indicated that P10–P14 synapses were significantly more depressed (PPR: 0.4 ± 0.1) than either P15–P18 (0.7 ± 0.2) or P19–P29 (0.8 ± 0.2).

span.label: sag —part-of→ FS
span.note: prominent only at P10-P14 and essentially gone later, so it is a property of the young cell rather than of the type
span.quote: In addition, at P10–P14, there was a prominent sag in response to hyperpolarizing steps (−50 pA, 1 s; Fig. 2 F , inset) consistent with the presence of I h

span.label: biocytin —operationalised-as→ FS
span.note: a third identification route alongside electrophysiology and the transgene, used on 72 cells
span.quote: Several neurons ( n = 72) were filled with biocytin to confirm their identity.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: Significance was assessed using univariate analysis of variance (ANOVA) with the Tukey's honestly significant difference post hoc test.

span.label: Tukey's HSD post hoc test
span.quote: Significance was assessed using univariate analysis of variance (ANOVA) with the Tukey's honestly significant difference post hoc test.

span.label: Levene's test for homogeneity of variance
span.term: Levene's test for homogeneity of variance
span.quote: Homogeneity of variances was confirmed at a <5% level using the Levene's test for homogeneity.

span.label: Mann-Whitney U test
span.quote: The nonparametric Mann–Whitney U test was used to assess significance of nonnormally distributed failure rates and for small data sets pertaining to comparisons between successive days in the P19–P29 range.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: All statistics are reported as mean ± standard deviation (SD).

span.label: least-squares curve fitting (chi-squared minimisation)
span.quote: All fits were performed using the Igor Pro, Levenberg-Marquardt nonlinear, least-squares fitting algorithm to search for the coefficient values that minimize chi-squared differences between the fit and data.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: These age-dependent decreases in τ d may, in part, be attributed to changes in the membrane time constant of the FS cells since the mean τ d and τ m at each age were linearly correlated ( R : 0.88, P < 0.01, Fig. 3 H ).

span.label: F statistic
span.quote: F values and P values are for ANOVA comparisons between multiple age groups.

span.label: Mann–Whitney U test
span.quote: As previously shown for PCs ( Oswald and Reyes 2008 ), both the intrinsic and the synaptic properties of FS cells undergo a transition between P10 and P18 and plateau between P19 and P29.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: As previously shown for PCs ( Oswald and Reyes 2008 ), both the intrinsic and the synaptic properties of FS cells undergo a transition between P10 and P18 and plateau between P19 and P29.

span.label: Between P10 and P29 the firing rates of fast-spiking interneurons rose, driven by shorter membrane time constants, briefer afterhyperpolarizations and narrower action potentials.
span.quote: FS cell firing rates increased with age owing to decreased membrane time constants, shorter afterhyperpolarizations, and narrower action potentials.

span.label: IPSP latency, rise time and peak time, together with the decay constants of both EPSPs and IPSPs, all shortened between P10 and P29.
span.quote: The latencies, rise, and peak times of the IPSPs, as well as the decay constants of both EPSPs and IPSPs decreased between P10 and P29.

span.label: Excitatory PC-to-FS synapses in the youngest animals depressed most strongly (paired-pulse ratio 0.4) and this depression weakened with age (0.7 at P15-P18 and 0.8 at P19-P29).
span.quote: The paired pulse ratios (10-Hz stimulation; PPR = EPSP 2 /EPSP 1 ) indicated that P10–P14 synapses were significantly more depressed (PPR: 0.4 ± 0.1) than either P15–P18 (0.7 ± 0.2) or P19–P29 (0.8 ± 0.2).

span.label: Because short-term depression at PC-to-FS synapses weakened with age, older synapses sustained their responses better during repetitive stimulation.
span.quote: In addition, decreases in short-term depression at excitatory PC–FS synapses resulted in more sustained synaptic responses during repetitive stimulation.

span.label: The temporal properties that determine when inhibition is recruited mature later than the corresponding properties of excitation.
span.quote: Finally, we show that during early development, the temporal properties that influence the recruitment of inhibition lag those of excitation.

span.label: IPSP amplitude fell from 0.8 mV at P10-P14 to 0.5 mV at P19-P29.
span.quote: IPSP amplitudes decreased from 0.8 ± 0.5 mV (P10–P14) to 0.5 ± 0.3 mV (P19–P29, P < 0.01; Fig. 4 A , B and Table 3 ).

span.label: The EPSP decay time constant shortened from 37 ms at P10-P14 to 16 ms at P19-P29 while the rise time constant did not change with age.
span.quote: Although τ r did not change with age (1.4 ± 0.9 ms, Table 2 ), the decay of the EPSP (τ d ) decreased significantly between P10–P14 (37 ± 26 ms) and P19–P29 (16 ± 8 ms, P < 0.01) ( Fig. 3 G ).

span.label: FS-to-PC inhibitory responses to single pulses were entirely GABA_A-receptor mediated, being abolished by bicuculline.
span.quote: Inhibitory responses evoked with single-stimulus pulses were completely blocked by the γ-aminobutyric acid A (GABA A ) receptor antagonist bicuculline (10 μM; Fig. 4 E , n = 16).

span.label: At resting potential, PC-to-FS excitatory responses were entirely AMPA-receptor mediated, being abolished by DNQX.
span.quote: In addition, at resting membrane potentials, the EPSPs were completely blocked by α-amino-3-hydroxyl-5-methyl-4-isoxazole-propionate (AMPA) receptor antagonist, DNQX ( n = 8; ages P14, P17, P18, and P22; Fig. 3 I ).

span.label: FS-cell intrinsic membrane and action-potential properties were indistinguishable between the GFP-expressing G42 line and Swiss Webster mice at every age tested.
span.quote: We found that the intrinsic membrane properties and AP properties ( Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 1 ) of the FS cells in our dataset did not differ between G42 and SW mice at any age.

span.label: Except for latency, inhibitory rise, peak and decay timescales were longer than the corresponding excitatory timescales at every age.
span.quote: With the exception of latency, inhibitory synaptic timescales—the rise, peak and decay of the IPSP—were significantly longer than excitatory timescales (FS–PC connections; open stars, Fig. 6 B – D ).

span.label: Fast-spiking cells at P10-P14 were the least mature electrically, with the longest membrane time constants, highest input resistance and most depolarized resting potential.
span.quote: The τ m , R n , and resting membrane potential ( V rest ) were the highest in neurons between P10 and P14 (τ m : 23 ± 11 ms; R n : 294 ± 183 MΩ; V rest : −63 ± 23 mV, P < 0.01; Fig. 2 D , E and Table 1 ).

span.label: input resistance and membrane time constant both fell sharply between P10-P14 and P19-P29
span.quote: Typically, FS cells in older animals (P15–P18, P19–P29; Fig. 1 , middle, right) have suprathreshold electrophysiological features that distinguish them from PCs and other interneurons ( Connors and Gutnick 1990 ). These include high nonadapting firing rates (ISI Last :ISI First : 1.09 ± 0.14, see Methods), a high rheobase (∼0.3), and narrow action potentials (half width, HW: 0.2–0.5 ms), with strong, brief afterhyperpolarizations

span.label: spikes narrowed and afterhyperpolarisations shortened with age, raising firing rates
span.quote: We found that the maturation of the intrinsic and synaptic properties of both FS cells and their connected PCs influence the timescales of inhibition. FS cell firing rates increased with age owing to decreased membrane time constants, shorter afterhyperpolarizations, and narrower action potentials.

span.label: the hyperpolarisation-activated sag was prominent only in the youngest cells
span.quote: In addition, at P10–P14, there was a prominent sag in response to hyperpolarizing steps (−50 pA, 1 s; Fig. 2 F , inset) consistent with the presence of I h

span.label: excitatory amplitudes fell with age and correlated with input resistance across all ages
span.quote: The mean and variability of EPSP amplitudes at PC-to-FS synapses decreased significantly between P10–P14 (1.8 ± 1.6 mV) and P19–P29 (1.1 ± 0.9 mV, P < 0.01; Fig. 3 A ). Over all ages, the mean amplitude was correlated with the input resistance

span.label: short-term depression at excitatory synapses weakened with age, making repetitive responses more sustained
span.quote: PC–FS synapses showed frequency-dependent short-term depression that decreased with age ( Fig. 3 B – D ). The paired pulse ratios (10-Hz stimulation; PPR = EPSP 2 /EPSP 1 ) indicated that P10–P14 synapses were significantly more depressed (PPR: 0.4 ± 0.1) than either P15–P18 (0.7 ± 0.2) or P19–P29 (0.8 ± 0.2).

span.label: inhibitory latencies, rise and peak times all shortened between P10 and P29
span.quote: The rise, peak, and decay times of the IPSPs decreased with age, which may, in part, be attributed to correlated decreases in membrane time constant of the postsynaptic PCs.

span.label: inhibitory decays stayed longer than excitatory ones at every age, setting an upper frequency bound
span.quote: We have shown that the decay constants of inhibitory synapses were significantly longer than excitation at all ages. This suggests that inhibition sets an upper frequency bound for responses to inputs arriving at short intervals. In young animals, IPSPs are approximately 60–200 ms long and can summate during repetitive ( Fig. 5 ) or asynchronous stimulation producing long-lasting hyperpolarizations that reduce responsiveness to frequencies >10 Hz. In older animals, decreased IPSP durations (25–50 ms) limit summation and increase neural responsiveness to higher input frequencies (20–40 Hz).

span.label: properties transitioned between P10 and P18 and plateaued from P19 to P29
span.quote: As previously shown for PCs ( Oswald and Reyes 2008 ), both the intrinsic and the synaptic properties of FS cells undergo a transition between P10 and P18 and plateau between P19 and P29.

span.label: excitatory potentials were fully blocked by an AMPA receptor antagonist
span.quote: The EPSPs (black) were completely blocked by the AMPA receptor antagonist DNQX (20 μM, gray, n = 8) at resting membrane potentials

span.label: CONTROL: GFP-labelled cells in the transgenic line and electrophysiologically identified cells did not differ at any age
span.quote: Since the majority of FS interneurons are PV+ ( Kawaguchi and Kondo 2002 ) and G42 mice express the EGFP transgene in (PV+) cells, we compared the properties of GFP+ interneurons recorded from G42 mice with FS cells recorded in SW mice of the same age. We found that the intrinsic membrane properties and AP properties ( Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 1 ) of the FS cells in our dataset did not differ between G42 and SW mice at any age.

span.label: UNEXPECTED RESULT: inhibitory potential amplitudes fell with age, where other cortical areas report the current rising
span.quote: There is also a modest but significant decrease in IPSP amplitude between P10 and P29. These results were somewhat unexpected given that IPSC amplitudes in other cortical areas increase with age ( Doischer et al. 2008 ; Kobayashi et al. 2008 ); α 1 GABA A receptor subunits have a higher peak current than α 3 subunits ( Gingrich et al. 1995 ) and GAD65 expression increases

span.label: RESOLUTION OFFERED: falling input resistance would convert a rising inhibitory current into a falling inhibitory voltage
span.quote: Alternatively, recent in vivo studies in AI have shown that inhibitory strength is stable throughout early development ( Dorrn et al. 2010 ; Sun et al. 2010 ). One likely explanation for our results is that correlated decreases in PC input resistance during development counter increases in IPSC amplitude.

span.label: the classification of fast-spiking cells is hardest exactly in the youngest animals, where the defining responses are less apparent
span.quote: The identification of FS cells based on electrophysiological properties can be difficult particularly in young animals (P10–P14) since “FS” responses are less apparent.

span.label: spike frequency adaptation (adaptation ratio)
span.quote: Spike frequency adaptation was quantified as the ratio of the last interspike interval (ISI Last ) to the first (ISI First ) in response to a depolarizing step current (1 s) that evoked firing rates of 40 ± 17 Hz.

span.label: failure rate
span.quote: The failure rate was determined as the number of failed trials divided by the total number of trials.

span.label: paired pulse ratio
span.quote: The paired pulse ratio was obtained from the trial-averaged traces and taken as the amplitude of the second PSP divided by the amplitude of the first.

span.label: EPSP latency
span.quote: The EPSP latency, defined as the time difference between the onset of the EPSP and the onset of the presynaptic AP, decreased with age between P15–P18 (1.1 ± 0.5 ms) and P19–P29 (0.9 ± 0.3 ms, P < 0.05) ( Table 2 ).

span.label: PSP latency
span.quote: PSP latency is defined as the difference between the onset of the PSP and the onset of the presynaptic action potential.

span.label: spike threshold
span.quote: Spike threshold was the membrane potential that corresponded to the maximum of the second derivative of the membrane voltage between baseline and the peak of the action potential.

span.label: sag amplitude
span.quote: The amplitude of the sag (the difference between the maximum [step onset] and minimum [step offset] membrane hyperpolarization) was significantly greater between P10–P14 (1.6 ± 1.3 mV) versus P15–P18 (0.3 ± 0.2 mV) or P19–P29 (0.2 ± 0.2 mV; Fig. 2 F ).

span.label: P10 to P29 — age range, spanning hearing onset to the plateau
span.quote: The time course of inhibition plays an important role in cortical sensitivity, tuning, and temporal response properties. We investigated the development of L2/3 inhibitory circuitry between fast-spiking (FS) interneurons and pyramidal cells (PCs) in auditory thalamocortical slices from mice between postnatal day 10 (P10) and P29.

span.label: 60-200 ms against 25-50 ms — inhibitory potential durations in young against older animals
span.quote: We have shown that the decay constants of inhibitory synapses were significantly longer than excitation at all ages. This suggests that inhibition sets an upper frequency bound for responses to inputs arriving at short intervals. In young animals, IPSPs are approximately 60–200 ms long and can summate during repetitive ( Fig. 5 ) or asynchronous stimulation producing long-lasting hyperpolarizations that reduce responsiveness to frequencies >10 Hz. In older animals, decreased IPSP durations (25–50 ms) limit summation and increase neural responsiveness to higher input frequencies (20–40 Hz).
